definition: Exhilarated means filled with a rush of energizing happiness — thrilled, wide awake, and charged with fresh energy.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word exhilarated. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know exhilarated should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Exhilarated by her first solo landing, Noor taxied in grinning and talking at twice her normal speed.
Pleased is far milder than exhilarated: a pleased person smiles and carries on, while an exhilarated one is charged — loud, quick, and hunting for the next hill.
Euphoric is stronger than exhilarated: exhilaration is a vivid, energizing rush that stays tethered to its cause, while euphoria floods everything, a high so total it can float free of reason.

Thrilled is the sudden jolt of excitement — the spike when the news lands. Exhilarated is the jolt plus the current that follows: energy still surging after the moment has passed, mind wide awake and body ready for more.

Invigorated means refreshed and restored to energy — a cold shower invigorates without any joy attached. Exhilarated runs on the same fresh energy but is unmistakably happy about it: the charge and the delight arrive together.

Exhilaration is joy with voltage in it.

The rafters aren't calmly satisfied; the thrill has flooded them with energy — racing pulses, loud voices, the itch to go again — and that electric, wide-awake charge is exactly what exhilarated adds to plain happy.
Exhilarated is the body's word for joy: pulse, breath, and voltage.
Elated, taught earlier in this unit, climbs high but can sit still; exhilaration never sits — it wants motion, another run, a colder wind.
Use it when the happiness is physical and freshly caused.
For quiet good moods it overclaims, and for a high so total it floats free of its cause, English usually reaches for euphoric instead.
